heading: JSON to C# Classes for .NET
subtitle: Open or paste JSON and C# classes for it appear at once, ready to copy or download as .cs; nothing is uploaded.
intro: Deserializing JSON in .NET goes faster when the model classes are already there. Open or paste a response and the page writes a public partial class for every object in it, inside namespace Example: PascalCase properties such as public long Id { get; set; }, long or double depending on the numbers in the sample, arrays such as string[] or Project[], and nullable types such as string? where some items leave a key out. Copy the classes into your project or download a .cs file. They are generated in your browser; the response is never uploaded.

handlesTitle: What the JSON to C# generator handles
handles: Properties: { get; set; } properties named in PascalCase, in public partial classes.
Numbers: long for whole numbers, double when a value has a decimal part.
Keys missing from some items: nullable types such as string? or bool?.
Arrays: typed by their items, such as string[] or Project[]; objects in one array merge into one class.
A value that is null everywhere in the sample becomes object.
Input from a .json file, a drop, the paste box or a sample, up to 10 MB.
limits: No attribute keeps the original JSON name; camelCase or snake_case keys need serializer options to match the PascalCase properties.
Types come from one sample: a property that is null in every item becomes object.
Numbers become long or double; switch to int or decimal by hand where your domain needs it, such as money.
Very large documents may take a few seconds; files up to 10 MB.
faqTitle: JSON to C# classes: questions and answers

faq.question: Is my file uploaded?
faq.answer: No. The JSON is read and the C# code is generated by your browser, on your device. Pasted text stays in this tab and is never sent anywhere.

faq.question: How do the classes handle nullable reference types?
faq.answer: Keys missing from some items get nullable types, such as string? or bool?. With <Nullable>enable</Nullable> in your project, read the compiler's warnings on the other reference properties and add ? or a default where your data can be empty.

faq.question: My JSON uses camelCase keys. How do they bind to PascalCase properties?
faq.answer: The classes carry no attributes, so tell the serializer. With System.Text.Json, set PropertyNameCaseInsensitive = true or PropertyNamingPolicy = JsonNamingPolicy.CamelCase in JsonSerializerOptions, and "orderId" fills OrderId.

faq.question: Why is a price typed double and not decimal?
faq.answer: JSON does not say which numeric type to use, so decimals become double. For money, change those properties to decimal by hand.

faq.question: Can I paste a JSON array of records?
faq.answer: Yes. The items are merged into one class: keys present in every item keep their plain type, keys missing from some items become nullable. Deserialize into an array of that class.

faq.question: Does it make records or classes?
faq.answer: Partial classes with get and set properties, which every .NET version and serializer reads. Turning them into records is a short edit if your project prefers them.

faq.question: How do I convert JSON to C# classes?
faq.answer: Paste a JSON sample into OpenAnyDoc's JSON to C# generator and the classes appear at once, one per kind of object with a property for every key. Copy them or download a .cs file, change the namespace to yours and deserialize into Root; the JSON stays in your browser.
